items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Plan **pl_003** is written and active. Here's the full FAN plan for **q_001 — Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 1908)?**

---

## Why a FAN plan was needed

The two completed plans searched only census co-residence (1850, 1860) and the 1908 death certificate. The death certificate named Thomas Flynn as father, but the informant was a **son-in-law** (James Brown) — secondary evidence from someone not present at the birth. The 1850/1860 censuses infer the relationship from household position; neither census stated it explicitly. And one assertion (a_009) shows Patrick was actually **born in Ireland**, contradicting the death certificate's "Pennsylvania" — further undermining the informant's reliability. Parentage is unproved.

The FAN pivot targets Thomas Flynn's own records, Patrick's records that would name his parents, and the immigration paper trail that placed the family together before 1850.

---

## Plan pl_003 — 9 items

| # | Type | What / Where | Period | Repository | Availability |
|---|------|-------------|--------|------------|--------------|
| pli_006 | Census | **1880 US Census** | 1880 | FamilySearch | name-searchable (personCount 50,169,452) |
| pli_007 | Census | **1870 US Census** | 1870 | FamilySearch | name-searchable (personCount 38,558,371) |
| pli_008 | Probate | **Thomas Flynn's will/estate**, Schuylkill Co. | 1860–1910 | FamilySearch | browse-only (personCount 0) — image group 007936749 |
| pli_009 | Church | **Thomas & wife's marriage**, Schuylkill Co. | 1830–1848 | FamilySearch | name-searchable (personCount 982,415) — SYNTH-PA-CHURCH |
| pli_010 | Church | Browse church register fallback *(fallback for pli_009)* | 1842–1895 | FamilySearch | browse-only (personCount 0) — image group 007936751 |
| pli_011 | Church | **Patrick's own marriage** (names groom's parents) | 1865–1885 | FamilySearch | name-searchable via SYNTH-PA-CHURCH |
| pli_012 | Immigration | **Thomas Flynn's naturalization papers**, Schuylkill Co. | 1849–1890 | FamilySearch | browse-only (personCount 0) — image group 007936750 |
| pli_013 | Immigration | **Passenger lists** — Flynn family Ireland → US | 1840–1850 | FamilySearch | indexed arrival manifests |
| pli_014 | Land | **Schuylkill County deeds** — Thomas's FAN cluster & any conveyance to Patrick | 1840–1900 | FamilySearch | 22% indexed — image group 007936752 |

---

## Why each item earns its place

**pli_006 — 1880 Census (first priority).** The 1880 census introduced the relationship column — something 1850 and 1860 lacked entirely. If Thomas is alive and Patrick still in the household, "son" is written on the line. This is the single fastest path to explicit relationship evidence not yet tried.

**pli_007 — 1870 Census.** Bridges the gap between the 1860 placement and Thomas's unknown death. May show Thomas still alive, identify his wife, or surface siblings who become their own FAN targets.

**pli_008 — Probate.** Thomas has no death record in the tree. A Schuylkill will naming Patrick as heir is direct parentage evidence; the estate purchasers and bondsmen expose Thomas's full FAN cluster.

**pli_009/010 — Thomas & wife's marriage.** Required on every parentage plan. Confirms the couple as a unit, supplies the mother's maiden name (omitted from every record found so far), and corroborates Thomas as father by date proximity to Patrick's ~1845 Irish birth. The couple may have married in Ireland before emigrating, so this item pairs with pli_013.

**pli_011 — Patrick's own marriage.** Patrick had a married daughter by 1908 (→ son-in-law informant). Pennsylvania Catholic marriage registers of this era named the groom's parents; a closer-in-time record from a better-positioned informant would independently corroborate Thomas as father.

**pli_012 — Naturalization.** Thomas was an Irish immigrant. Post-1906 naturalization forms required naming wife and children; pre-1906 petitions sometimes did. A naturalization record naming Patrick among Thomas's dependents is family-placement evidence from a governmental source.

**pli_013 — Passenger lists.** The family was in Schuylkill County by 1850 and came from Ireland. An arrival manifest showing Thomas Flynn with a wife and child named Patrick is the strongest possible proof that Patrick traveled as a member of Thomas's family — direct and original.

**pli_014 — Deeds.** Two FAN uses: a conveyance "Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn, my son" is direct; boundary recitals naming adjoining landowners map Thomas's neighbor cluster and may reveal Flynn relatives invisible in the census.

---

## Fallback relationship

If pli_009 (name-searchable church records) returns no Flynn marriage → execute **pli_010** (browse the unindexed 1842–1895 church register image group).

---

## Suggested next step

Execute **pli_006** first — the 1880 census is name-searchable, free, and the fastest route to an explicitly-stated relationship. Would you like me to run the search now?

## Research Plan `pl_003` — *Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 1908)?*

**Context:** The prior plan (`pl_002`) established Thomas Flynn as *probably* Patrick's father — two censuses (1850, 1860) show them in the same household, and a death certificate names Thomas as father, but all three yield only indirect or secondary evidence. The proof summary (`ps_001`) is rated **Probable** and explicitly names what would move it to **Proved**: the 1870/1880/1900 censuses and Thomas Flynn's probate. The project tree has **no mother for Patrick at all** — her identity is a second open gap this plan addresses.

---

### Execution order

| # | Item | Record type | Repository | Availability | Date range |
|---|------|-------------|------------|--------------|------------|
| 1 | **pli_006** | 1880 Census — Thomas & Patrick Flynn | Census | FamilySearch | 1880 |
| 2 | **pli_007** | 1870 Census — Thomas & Patrick Flynn | Census | FamilySearch | 1870 |
| 3 | **pli_008** | Thomas Flynn probate / will | Probate | FamilySearch | 1870–1900 |

| 8 | **pli_013** | Church records browse *(fallback → pli_009)* | Church | FamilySearch | 1840–1865 |

### Item rationales

**1 · pli_006 — 1880 Census (FamilySearch, collection 1417683, name-searchable personCount 50,169,452)**
The 1880 census was the *first* U.S. census to state each person's relationship to the head of household. Two searches are needed: Thomas Flynn (~62) and Patrick Flynn (~35, likely now his own household head). If Thomas is alive and Patrick is in his household, this census could explicitly record "son" for the first time — no inference needed. Even in separate households, Thomas's wife is named with her age and birthplace, finally identifying Patrick's probable mother (currently absent from the project tree). Test Flyn and Flinn variants.

**2 · pli_007 — 1870 Census (FamilySearch, collection 1438024, name-searchable personCount 38,558,371)**
Fills the gap between 1860 (Patrick age 15 in Thomas's household) and 1880. Thomas (~52) may still head the same Schuylkill household; Patrick (~25) may still be present or nearby. The relationship column isn't yet present, but a third decade of co-residence significantly strengthens the indirect chain. Thomas's wife appears by name — another route to the unknown mother.

**3 · pli_008 — Thomas Flynn probate (FamilySearch, collection 1999196, browse-only personCount 0; volume 007936749, Schuylkill 1851–1930)**
A will naming Patrick as a son is *direct* parentage evidence — the proof summary says explicitly this would advance the conclusion to Proved. The `loc_001` locality entry confirms Schuylkill's Register of Wills holds probate from 1811. Both the statewide collection and the county volume are browse-only, so this is an image browse. Date window is Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan (b. ~1818), not Patrick's — he could have died anytime from the early 1870s to mid-1890s.

**4 · pli_009 — Thomas & wife's marriage, church records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable personCount 982,415)**
Mandatory for a parentage plan. The record (a) confirms the couple as a unit; (b) gives the wife's maiden name — currently *entirely unknown* in the project tree; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 Ireland birth, corroborates Thomas as husband and father. They may have married in Ireland before immigration, but a search of Schuylkill County church registers is warranted if they arrived unmarried. Important limit: this record proves *they* married — it does not establish Patrick is *their* child; a record placing him with them remains needed.

**5 · pli_010 — 1900 Census (FamilySearch, collection 1325221, name-searchable personCount 76,211,837)**
The 1900 schedule records each person's father's birthplace and mother's birthplace. For Patrick (~55), both columns should read Ireland, consistent with Thomas Flynn's documented Irish origin — corroborating the parentage identification and anchoring Patrick's continued Schuylkill County residence eight years before his 1908 death.

**6 · pli_011 — Thomas Flynn land/deed records (volume 007936752, Schuylkill 1815–1900, 22% indexed)**
The required FAN item for this parentage question. Deed boundary recitals name adjoining landowners — neighbors and frequently kin — and estate-sale purchasers are a second FAN cluster. A deed with Patrick as co-grantor or named heir is collateral parentage evidence. 22% of pages are indexed; a name search runs first, a browse of the un-indexed pages follows if needed. Date window set by Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan as a Schuylkill property owner.

**7 · pli_012 — Thomas Flynn probate, Ancestry *(fallback for pli_008)***

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (S3, cert. no. 4521) is already in the project and cited as supporting both his death fact (F2) and the Thomas–Patrick parent-child relationship (R1). Pennsylvania death certificates issued after 1906 require the informant to report the father's and mother's names. No parental name assertions have been extracted from S3 for q_001 — BCG Standard 11 caution: Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father is currently supported only by inferred household co-residence in the 1850 census (a_004); S3 is cited as supporting R1 but its parental content has not been documented as an assertion. Reading cert. no. 4521 for the father and mother fields is the single highest-probability action to directly identify both parents. Spelling variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn, Flyne.

The 1860 U.S. Federal Census (S2, dwelling 112, Schuylkill Co.) is already in the project and cited in R1, but no household assertions for q_001 have been extracted from it. The 1860 census records all household members with names, ages, and birthplaces; household order places a wife typically after the head. Thomas's wife — Patrick's mother — would appear here if alive in 1860. Patrick, ~15 in 1860, would also appear if still in the household. Collection 1473181 (United States Census, 1860) is name-searchable (personCount 27,518,891). Search Thomas Flynn and cross-check against dwelling 112 in Schuylkill County. Spelling variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

Dedicated item — the marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife (Patrick's mother) to each other. Their marriage record: (a) confirms the couple as a unit; (b) supplies the wife's surname, which census and death records usually omit; (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845), corroborates Thomas as father — a claim currently resting only on inferred co-residence in a single census. If the family was Catholic (as the Irish immigrant anthracite mining community predominantly was), the register is in a Schuylkill County Catholic parish held under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable (personCount 982,415) and covers 1708-1985. Search Thomas Flynn as groom; also search the wife's surname once identified from item 1. If the marriage predates emigration (~1845 or earlier), the register may be in Ireland — begin with the Pennsylvania Catholic records, then extend to Irish records once the origin parish is identified. Note: this marriage proves the couple wed; it does not, by itself, establish that Patrick is their child — that link requires a record placing Patrick with the parents (items 1, 2, 4).

S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is already in the project's sources list but has no associated assertions, fact references, or relationship references — it may be Thomas Flynn's will or estate administration. A will naming Patrick as a son is direct parentage evidence; an administration naming heirs establishes the same; either would also name a surviving wife (Patrick's mother) or identify other children as siblings. Thomas was born ~1818 in Ireland; the date range 1855–1910 spans his plausible death window — Thomas's lifespan sets the upper bound, not Patrick's research window. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1999196) returns personCount 0 — browse-only; image browsing of volume 007936749 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, 1851-1930, 0% record-searchable) is required. Begin by reading S4 to extract any assertions; if S4 does not correspond to Thomas Flynn, browse volume 007936749 for a Flynn probate entry in the relevant years.

Thomas Flynn would be ~52 in 1870; if his wife (Patrick's mother) was still alive, she would appear in the household by name, age, and birthplace. Patrick, ~25 in 1870, may or may not remain in the parental household. Collection 1438024 (United States Census, 1870) is name-searchable (personCount 38,558,371). Finding the household corroborates the parent-child link and may identify the mother if she does not appear on the 1908 death certificate (item 1) or the 1860 census (item 2). Spelling variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

The 1880 U.S. Federal Census is the first to explicitly name each person's relationship to the head of household. If Thomas Flynn (age ~62) is alive and Patrick (~35) remains in or visits the household, the relationship column would directly state 'son' — the most direct census statement of parentage in the available record set. If Thomas has died and Patrick heads his own household, the 1880 census records each person's father's and mother's birthplaces, corroborating Irish origin on both sides. Collection 1417683 (United States Census, 1880) is name-searchable (personCount 50,169,452). Spelling variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

Baptism entries for Patrick's siblings in Schuylkill County Catholic registers would directly name Thomas Flynn and his wife (Patrick's mother) as parents. Patrick was born in Ireland ~1845 and his own baptism is not expected in Pennsylvania records; younger siblings born after the family's arrival (~1847 onward) would be baptized locally. A sibling's baptism entry names both parents — identifying the mother even if she does not survive in any census. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable (personCount 982,415). Search for children of Thomas Flynn or (once identified) the wife's surname. This item is a fallback for item 3 (Thomas's marriage): if no marriage entry for Thomas survives in the Schuylkill County registers, a child's baptism entry naming both parents achieves the same identification of the mother.

Patrick Flynn was born ~1845 and was 16-20 during the Civil War. An enlistment record may state a more specific birthplace than 'Ireland' and may name next of kin or a father. A pension file, if Patrick served, can contain depositions from family members directly corroborating the parent-child relationship. The 1863 draft registration covered males aged 20-45; Patrick at 18 in 1863 was just below threshold but may appear in 1864-1865 registrations at age 19-20. Collection 1932430 (United States, Civil War Service Records, 1861-1865) is name-searchable (personCount 6,443,102). Spelling variants: Flynn, Flyn, Flinn.

Naturalization declarations and petitions often state the applicant's county or townland of birth in Ireland — the critical detail needed to locate Thomas and Patrick Flynn's home parish, which is the prerequisite for seeking baptism and marriage records abroad. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 in Ireland) would have filed a declaration of intent after arrival (~1847 or later); Patrick (born ~1845, present in Pennsylvania by 1850) would have declared intent at age 21+ (~1866 onward). Volume 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849-1915) is browse-only (personCount 0): records require image-by-image browsing. Once a specific Irish county or townland is identified, the search-full-text skill can execute a co-occurrence search on 'Flynn' and any correlated surname across FamilySearch's AI-transcribed Irish parish corpus — the highest-yield route to the parents' baptism or marriage record in Ireland.

FAN cluster item — required for a parentage question. The households adjacent to Thomas Flynn's in the 1850 census (dwelling 84) and 1860 census (dwelling 112) likely include Irish-born families who emigrated from the same townland or parish. Chain migration was the dominant settlement pattern for the Schuylkill County anthracite coal region; a neighbor's naturalization record, obituary, or church transfer naming a specific Irish parish or county directly bears on the question — it points to the locality where Thomas and his wife married. This item is a fallback for item 9 (naturalization): if Thomas's and Patrick's naturalization papers cannot be located or give only 'Ireland,' neighboring households in the same dwelling block offer an alternate path to the same information. Collections 1473181 (1860, name-searchable, personCount 27,518,891) and the indexed 1850 U.S. Federal Census are used to identify neighboring households.

Swedish Lutheran marriage entries from this period recorded the bride's home parish and frequently her father's name — the highest-probability indexed source for her parentage. Variants to search: Elena/Helena/Elin/Lena; Asmundsdotter abbreviated d., dr., dtr. The tree records the marriage event (R1) but the original record has not been examined.

Sweden, Malmöhus, Church Records (collection 1974200) is browse-only (personCount 0). Image group 004523018 covers Västra Karaby 1688–1804 and also includes the 004523021 group that begins 1662. Browse to the 29 December 1712 marriage entry directly in the handwritten register — detail that did not make it into the national index (bride's home parish, father's name) is likely present in the original.

Sweden, Baptisms, 1611-1920 (collection 1520594) is name-searchable (personCount 20057677). The Västra Karaby baptism register begins in 1688 (loc_002); a birth in the later portion of Elena's estimated window (ca. 1688–1692) may have an indexed entry naming her father Asmund. Search Malmöhus/Västra Karaby for Elena/Helena/Elin/Lena with surname Asmundsdotter and abbreviations (d., dr., dtr.). A baptism entry is direct evidence of parentage.

Sweden, Malmöhus, Church Records (collection 1974200) is browse-only (personCount 0). If the national baptisms index yields no match, browse image group 004523018 (Västra Karaby, 1688–1804) page by page for baptisms ca. 1688–1695, looking for any child christened as Elena/Helena/Elin/Lena with father named Asmund. The national index is partial (loc_002 notes that coverage is incomplete), so a browse may recover entries the index misses.

Sweden, Burials, 1649-1920 (collection 1520597) is name-searchable (personCount 2861902). Planned per the rule that the subject's own burial entry must be searched when no baptism can be expected: Elena's birth (ca. 1680–1692) may predate Västra Karaby's 1688 register start, leaving her burial as the primary independent source for her age and home parish. Swedish Lutheran burial entries of this period routinely recorded the deceased's age and origin parish. Elena died in Barsebäck (the couple's parish from at least 1718); search the Barsebäck area for Asmundsdotter or Elena Jönsdotter (she might be listed under her married designation).

Sweden, Malmöhus, Church Records (collection 1974200) is browse-only (personCount 0). If the national burials index returns no match, browse image groups 004514823 and 004514824 (Barsebäck, 1648 onward; loc_001) for Elena's burial entry. The Barsebäck register is complete from 1648; her burial falls somewhere in 1713–1760 (she was alive in 1718 at her son Asmund's christening). The entry may state her age at death and her home parish, yielding an independent birth estimate and confirming Västra Karaby as her origin.

Sweden, Malmöhus, Church Records (collection 1974200) is browse-only (personCount 0). Required FAN item for a parentage question. Browse image group 004523018 (Västra Karaby, 1688–1804) for any baptism entry listing a father named 'Asmund.' Each such entry names both parents: the father Asmund (with his own patronymic, which is otherwise unknown) and the mother (Elena's mother, whose given name is not yet documented). A sibling's baptism is direct evidence about Elena's parents as a couple and supplies the father's full name. Date range is bounded by the register start (1688) and Elena's 1712 marriage, with a modest extension to 1715 in case a younger sibling was baptized after Elena left the household. Date window is set by the parents' plausible childbearing years, not Elena's own research window.

Mantalslängder (annual household tax lists) for Harjager härad survive from 1658 and are held at Riksarkivet, searchable at https://sok.riksarkivet.se/mantalslangder (loc_002). These lists name each household head annually. If Elena's father Asmund headed a household in Västra Karaby ca. 1675–1712, he will appear recorded under his own patronymic (i.e., 'Asmund [father's name]son'), which identifies his father's given name and anchors the family unit in the parish before the church register begins. This is the primary source for the 1680–1687 birth window, predating the Västra Karaby register. Date window is set by Asmund's plausible lifespan as household head, estimated ca. 1658 (list start) through roughly 1715 (his likely death); not capped at Elena's marriage year since his household would persist after she left it.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.
Roman Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Scranton was erected in 1868; sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
